lead: Read the hidden metadata inside photos, videos, documents and many other files, such as camera model, dates and GPS position. ExifTool is a command-line program and Perl library written by Phil Harvey.
use_when: You need to know when, where and with what device a photo or video was made.
You want to compare the metadata of many files and put it in a spreadsheet.
You need to check what personal data a file would reveal, or remove it before sharing.

features.title: Reads metadata
items: Reads EXIF, GPS, IPTC, XMP, JFIF, ICC Profile, ID3 and other metadata types
Reads the maker notes of many camera brands, including Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm and GoPro
Supports hundreds of file types, such as JPEG, PNG, TIFF, HEIC, RAW camera files, PDF, MP4, MOV, MP3 and Office documents
Can show tag names in groups so you see where each value is stored

features.title: Works on many files at once
items: Processes whole folders and, with an option, all sub-folders
Can limit work to chosen file extensions
Can process only files that match a condition on a tag value
Can pull data out of embedded documents inside a file

features.title: Output you can use
items: Prints plain text, tab-separated tables, HTML, XML, JSON and CSV
Lets you choose the date format and build your own print layout
Shows GPS values as degrees or as decimal numbers
Can compare the metadata of two files

features.title: Writes and edits metadata
items: Sets, changes or deletes single tags, whole tag groups or all metadata
Copies tags from one file to another, even between different formats
Shifts date and time values and can geotag pictures from a GPS track log
Can rename or sort files by values taken from their metadata

formats: RAW camera files (for example CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG)
requirements: On Windows you can use a stand-alone program that already contains Perl. On macOS there is an installer package. On other systems you need Perl, which most already have. It runs from the command line, so you need a command window or terminal. No special hardware is needed.

steps.title: Download
steps.text: Go to exiftool.org and download the version for your system. On Windows choose the 32-bit or 64-bit zip. On macOS use the package. On Linux and other systems use the full distribution archive.

steps.title: Install on Windows
steps.text: Unzip the download. Rename the file exiftool(-k).exe to exiftool.exe. Keep it together with the exiftool_files folder, because the program needs it. Put both in a folder that is on your PATH, or note the full path to the file.

steps.title: Check that it runs
steps.text: Open a command window or terminal and print the version number. If you see a number, the install works.

steps.title: Read one file
steps.text: Run ExifTool with a file name. It prints all the metadata it can find. Look for the camera model, the date fields and any GPS position.

steps.title: Show where each value comes from
steps.text: Add the group option so every line shows its group name. Add the duplicates and unknown-tags options to see more. This helps you tell apart values stored in different places in the same file.

steps.title: Export a whole folder to CSV
steps.text: Run it on a folder with the recursive option and write CSV to a file. Open the CSV in a spreadsheet and sort by date or by camera. Always work on a copy of the evidence, not the original.

steps.title: Get GPS as decimal numbers
steps.text: Use the no-conversion option so coordinates print as plain decimal values that you can paste into a mapping tool.

options.what: Processes only files with this extension. Use --ext to leave an extension out.
Prints the result as CSV. With =file.csv it imports values from a CSV file instead.
Shows the group name in front of each tag.
Shows duplicate tags and tags the tool does not know by name.
Turns off value conversion, for example to see raw numbers and decimal GPS.
Also reads embedded documents inside a file.
When writing, do not keep a backup. Without it the original is kept with _original added to its name.
Keeps the file modification date unchanged when you write tags.

cases.title: Where and when a photo was taken
cases.why: Date tags and GPS tags can show a time and a place. You can compare them with other evidence.

cases.title: Which device made a file
cases.why: Make, model and maker note values can link several pictures to one camera or phone.

cases.title: Document authorship
cases.why: PDF and Office files can carry author names, software names and creation dates.

cases.title: Spotting edited pictures
cases.why: Software names, extra metadata blocks and date values that do not match can be a reason to look closer.

cases.title: Large sets of files
cases.why: One command can export the metadata of thousands of files to one CSV for sorting and filtering.

cases.title: Privacy checks and clean-up
cases.why: You can see which personal data a file would reveal, and delete tags from a copy before sharing it.

strengths: Free and open source, and it runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Supports a very wide range of file types and metadata formats, which the project lists on its home page.
Output goes to CSV, JSON, XML or HTML, so other tools can use it.
Detailed documentation of every option and every tag name is published.
limits: It has no graphical window. You must type commands, and the first days need practice.
It reads metadata only. It does not recover deleted files or look at disk images.
Metadata is easy to change or remove, so a missing or odd value is not proof of anything alone.
Writing changes files. Work on copies and keep the original evidence untouched.
By default, writing a tag changes the file modification date unless you use the preserve option.
On Windows, file names with special characters may need extra options. The FAQ explains the character set options.
Support differs by format. Some formats can be read but not written.
